claims.text: The local source slice models two Pokemon Card Trainers Vol. 10 insert rows: Dark Ivysaur row 225 and Dark Venusaur row 226.
The local source rows derive from Bulbapedia raw wikitext rows 225-226, both carrying the promotion note Pokemon Card Trainers Vol. 10 insert (March 1, 2001).

Bulbapedia's card pages say the Japanese prints were included in Volume 10 of Pokemon Card Trainers magazine and feature a GB symbol in place of an expansion symbol, referencing Pokemon Trading Card Game 2: The Invasion of Team GR!
Bulbapedia describes the prints as using the Neo Series layout and the aesthetic differences common to Dark Pokemon cards from this period.
Bulbapedia categorizes both Dark Ivysaur and Dark Venusaur as illustrated by Shin-ichi Yoshida.

This source group matters because it is not merely a magazine freebie: it is a physical bridge between Pokemon Card Trainers, the Game Boy Color Team GR sequel, and late Neo-era Dark Pokemon visual language.

Agents should preserve Pokemon Card Trainers Vol. 10 route, March 1 2001 date, rows 225-226 pair identity, GB-symbol print context, Team GR tie, Neo/Dark Pokemon layout context, Yoshida credit, Dark Venusaur holofoil caveat, and non-equivalence with Pokemon Web, Best of Game, Winner-stamped, Jumbo, Rocket, and generic Venusaur-line memories before accepting a match.

narrative.human_title: Pokemon Card Trainers Vol. 10 — Team GR leaks out of the Game Boy
narrative.why_it_matters: This release has that lovely late-WoC Japanese feeling where the card game, the magazines, and the Game Boy games are all talking to each other. Dark Ivysaur and Dark Venusaur are not just darker versions of familiar Grass evolutions. They are magazine-carried artifacts from the Team GR moment, with a GB symbol where a normal expansion symbol would sit and Neo-era Dark Pokemon design language around them. The route matters because the cards later echo through Pokemon Web, Best of Game, Winner-stamped, and Jumbo memories. A good agent should see the Venusaur-line gravity, then keep the magazine and Game Boy hinge intact.

narrative.human_title: Dark Ivysaur — the middle evolution that keeps the route honest
narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Ivysaur is easy to under-love next to Dark Venusaur, but it is the card that makes this release feel assembled rather than merely chased. It says: this was a pair, an evolution line fragment, a Team GR magazine moment. The GB symbol and Neo-era Dark Pokemon look are doing protocol work here; they keep the row out of generic Rocket or Pokemon Web memory. Shin-ichi Yoshida's art gives the card that rougher Dark Pokemon energy without making later reprints equivalent.

narrative.human_title: Dark Venusaur — the holofoil Team GR bloom
narrative.why_it_matters: Dark Venusaur has the easy gravity: starter final evolution, holofoil, villain-era aura. But the important part is how it was assembled. This is not Base Venusaur nostalgia in a black coat. It is Team GR videogame memory entering the paper TCG through Pokemon Card Trainers Vol. 10, marked by a GB symbol and Shin-ichi Yoshida's Dark Pokemon texture. Later English and web-era echoes make the card feel familiar; the magazine route is what makes it precise.
